papers.title_in_file: Classical and quantum machine learning applications in spintronics
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section II C, Section III A, Table I, Section IV conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A study that predicts conductance and spin response in a two-terminal magnetic-impurity device with classical random forests and a quantum SVM discussion.

assertions.value: The authors state that converting the conventional regression problem into a discretised classification problem gives a high level of accuracy even in a strongly nonlinear regime.
quotes: Our approach allows us to obtain a high level of accuracy even for a strongly nonlinear regime.
by converting the conventional regression problem into a discretised classiﬁcation problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one simulated device.

assertions.value: The authors state that the samples were randomly split into 9 × 104 training data and 104 testing data, with 50 different train-test cycles, and that random forest was used throughout.
assertions.anchor: Section III A, Success rate vs accuracy with number of classes
quotes: The samples are randomly split into 9 × 104 training data and 104 testing data and then we conduct 50 different train-test cycles.
Among these methods Random forest shows better performance within reasonable execution time, and therefore we use Random forest throughout the rest of the study.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section III A.

assertions.value: The authors state that the overall complexity of the quantum SVM is O (log(NM)), whereas classical complexity of the SVM is O M2 (M + N) , where N is the dimension of the feature space and M is the number of training vectors.
quotes: The overall complexity of the quantum SVM is O (log(NM)), whereas classical complexity of the SVM is O M2 (M + N) , where N is the dimension of the feature space and M is the number of training vectors.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the quantum SVM to cited work [47, 48]; the comparison is not derived in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The complexity comparison assumes QRAM access, which the paper mentions but does not cost.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum machine learning performs quite well for their small feature space, and claim that QML will be the only viable option for a larger configuration space and data size.
quotes: We further demonstrate the applicability of quantum machine learning which performs quite well for our small feature space.
in fact QML will be the only viable option in that regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about scaling; the larger regime is not tested in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The quantum demonstration is on a small feature space; the advantage at scale is asserted, not shown.

papers.title_in_file: A supervised hybrid quantum machine learning solution to the emergency escape routing problem
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section III C and III A, Fig. 4, Section V conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A study that trains a hybrid quantum-classical FiLM network to imitate node-wise Dijkstra routing on a simulated earthquake city graph.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical NN reaches an average accuracy of 87% and the HQNN 94%, and describe this as the HQNN predicting a path 7% closer to the node-wise Dijkstra's predicted path.
assertions.anchor: Section III A Results, Fig. 4, p.8
quotes: The classical NN model reaches an average accuracy of 87% and an arrival rate of 95%, showing the capability of mimicking Dijkstra’s algorithm.
The HQNN model significantly improved over the classical NN model, achieving an average accuracy of 94%.
This means that, on average, the HQNN model predicts a path 7% closer to the node-wise Dijkstra’s predicted path.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one city graph.
assertions.reader_inference: One graph and one dataset; the 7% gap has no variance estimate in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum network has seven qubits in total, five of which encode the system’s main features, and two that process the earthquake coordinates with a data reuploading circuit.
assertions.anchor: Section III C Hybrid Supervised Learning Architecture, p.6
quotes: The quantum network is created similarly, where there are seven qubits in total, five of which encode the system’s main features
The other two qubits process the earthquake coordinates using a data reuploading circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model setup in Section III C.

assertions.value: The authors state that the approach was tested on hypothetical situations on a concrete city graph, and that future research needs to focus on testing the approach on different and larger graphs.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section V Conclusion, p.1 and p.10
quotes: We propose a novel hybrid supervised learning approach and test it on hypothetical situations on a concrete city graph.
Future research needs to focus on testing the approach on different and larger graphs
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own test in the abstract and the conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: Computing Graph Edit Distance with Algorithms on Quantum Devices
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, experiments (Sections V and VI, Tables II and V), concluding remarks.
papers.what_it_is: A study that gives a QUBO formulation of graph edit distance and tests it on D-Wave annealers and on simulated VQE and QAOA against simulated annealing.

assertions.value: The authors state that both quantum annealers perform worse than simulated annealing, and that they can state the superior performance of classical hardware compared to the current quantum annealers for the GED problem.
quotes: Both quantum annealers perform worse than SA.
We can state the superior performances of classical hardware compared to the current quantum annealers, for the GED problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on small graphs.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion holds for the small graph sizes tested; no scaling beyond n = 9 is shown.

assertions.value: The authors report that variational algorithms were tested on graphs with at most 5 vertices (a circuit of 25 qubits), that the classical approach leads to much better solutions, and that no variational approaches are able to find an exact solution for instances having n ≥ 4 vertices.
assertions.anchor: Section VI C, Comparing variational algorithms, p.11
quotes: we have tested the variational approach on instances of GED with graphs having at most 5 vertices (thus our circuit uses 25 qubits).
For these small dimensions, the classical approach leads to much better solutions.
no variational approaches are able to ﬁnd an exact solution for instances having n ≥ 4 vertices.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from noiseless simulation of one problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the variational approach they used noiseless simulators, and that they report some preliminary evidences that the main variational algorithms may not be suited for the type of problem addressed.
quotes: We remark that, concerning the variational approach, we have used noiseless simulators
In this work we have reported some preliminary evidences that the main variational algorithms may not be suited for the type of problems as the one we have addressed in this paper.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope and limit of its own variational study in Section VII.

assertions.value: The authors state that D-Wave 2000Q has 2041 qubits and D-Wave Advantage 1.1 has 5436 qubits.
assertions.anchor: Section V B, D-Wave quantum annealers, p.7
quotes: D-Wave 2000Q has 2041 qubits and uses Chimera topology having 5974 couplers
D-Wave Advantage 1.1 has 5436 qubits and uses a Pegasus topology having 37440 couplers
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the hardware used in its own experiments.

papers.title_in_file: Benchmarking Quantum Generative Learning: A Study on Scalability and Noise Resilience using QUARK
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Sections II to V including Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Table I.
papers.what_it_is: A benchmarking study of QCBM and QGAN training under finite-shot and simulated hardware noise using the QUARK framework.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QGAN converges with more than one order of magnitude fewer circuit executions than the QCBM, to a KL divergence limit of 0.14 ± 0.01, against 0.49 ± 0.13 and 0.44 ± 0.12 for the QCBM at two shot budgets.
assertions.anchor: Section IV A Discussion, Fig. 2, p.4
quotes: The QGAN achieves faster convergence than the QCBM, requiring more than one order of magnitude fewer circuit
from CKcoLnv = 0.49 ± 0.13 to CKcoLnv = 0.44 ± 0.12.
divergence of the QGAN converges to a lower limit with a value CKcoLnv = 0.14 ± 0.01.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The two models use different optimizers (CMA-ES against gradient descent), so the comparison mixes model and optimizer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scaling comparison used a copula circuit with 12 qubits and a depth of one, fitted to one dataset resembling the letter X on the noise-free Qiskit AerSimulator, and that they used only one dataset.
assertions.anchor: Section IV A Experimental Design and Limitations, p.3 to p.4
quotes: We fitted the copula circuit with 12 qubits and a depth of one to a dataset resembling the shape of the letter X, using the quantum noise-free Qiskit AerSimulator.
Furthermore, we used only one dataset;
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup and limit of its own experiment in Section IV A.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QCBM performance is still below the random baseline for 6 qubits and pdepol = 0.2, and that for 12 qubits the model performance corresponds to random guessing already for pdepol = 0.1.
assertions.anchor: Section IV B Discussion, Fig. 3, p.4
quotes: The performance is still below the random baseline for 6 qubits and pdepol = 0.2.
For 12 qubits, however, the model performance corresponds to random guessing already for pdepol = 0.1.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from noisy simulation in one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that their studies of noise on QCBM training are limited to readout and two-qubit depolarizing errors, and that extending their studies to different quantum generative models, such as QGANs, would be interesting.
quotes: Our studies on the influence of noise on the training of QCBMs are limited to readout and two-qubit depolarizing errors.
Furthermore, extending our studies to different quantum generative models, such as QGANs, would be interesting.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own noise study in the conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: A new quantum machine learning algorithm: split hidden quantum Markov model inspired by quantum conditional master equation
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Sections 4, 5 and 6 (results table and discussion); supplemental material not available in the file.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and numerical-experiment paper that introduces the split hidden quantum Markov model (SHQMM) and a learning algorithm for it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experimental results suggest their model outperforms previous models in terms of scope of applications and robustness.
quotes: The experimental results suggest that our model outperforms previous models in terms of scope of applications and robustness.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in the abstract; the comparison data sit in a table and in supplemental material.

assertions.value: The authors report that for different sequences the model maintains STD(DA) < 0.01.
quotes: For different sequences, the model maintains STD(DA) < 0.01.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; numerical results are in the supplemental material.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current results are likely to be overfitted given the complexity of the relationship between a complex model and simple data with lower number and dimensionality of hidden states, and that SHQMM's performance with some classical datasets appears suboptimal.
assertions.anchor: Section 4 Result and Section 5, p.10 to p.11
quotes: The current results are likely to be overfitted given the complexity of the relationship between complex model and simple data with lower number and dimensionality of hidden states
It is noteworthy, however, that SHQMM’s performance with some classical datasets appears suboptimal.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limits of its own results in Sections 4 and 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that in numerical experiments on classical computers the results did not fully reflect the advantage that the complexity analysis suggests for larger n.
quotes: It should be acknowledged that in numerical experiments on classical computers, the results did not fully reflect this advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit of its own experiments in Section 5.

papers.title_in_file: Towards Optimizations of Quantum Circuit Simulation for Solving Max-Cut Problems with QAOA
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section 3 evaluation (text; table and figure values not read), Section 4 conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A systems paper that speeds up classical state-vector simulation of QAOA for max-cut using algebraic compression, bitwise operations and parallelism.

assertions.value: The authors report that their simulator surpasses QuEST by a factor of 17 on a virtual quantum computer running on a 16-core, 32-thread AMD Ryzen 9 5950X processor, with up to 438x speedups for the cost layer of a single-level QAOA circuit.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section 4 Conclusion, p.1 and p.6
quotes: surpassing a state-of-the-art simulator, QuEST, by a factor of 17 on a virtual quantum computer running on a 16-core, 32-thread AMD Ryzen 9 5950X processor.
our work achieves up to 438x speedups for the cost layer of a single-level QAOA circuit and up to 17x speedups for the five-level QAOA circuit on the multicore processor.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical benchmark from one study on one machine.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup measures classical simulation time of a quantum circuit; it is not a quantum advantage claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that the five-level QAOA is used as the input to QuEST and to their simulator, with the qubit size ranging from 21 to 30, and with the state vectors kept in 128 GB of the main memory.
quotes: The five-level QAOA is used as the input to QuEST and our simulator with the qubit size ranging from 21 to 30, where the state vectors are kept in 128 GB of the main memory.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own benchmark setup in Section 3.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the qubit size is larger than 24, the quantum states cannot be accommodated by the L3 cache of the processor (64 MB).
quotes: It is important to note that when the qubit size is larger than 24, the quantum states cannot be accommodated by the L3 cache of the processor (64 MB).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a hardware limit on its own benchmark in Section 3.2.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum algorithms for matrix geometric means
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I A, II, V and VI; proofs in the appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that gives quantum subroutines for matrix geometric means and algebraic Riccati equations, with applications to metric learning and fidelity estimation.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Theorem 21) that MGM(poly(n), poly(n)), a decision problem about a property of the matrix geometric mean of two well-conditioned sparse matrices, is BQP-complete.
quotes: Theorem 21. MGM(poly(n), poly(n)) is BQP-complete.
Roughly speaking, this problem pertains to testing a certain property of the matrix geometric mean of two well-conditioned sparse matrices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 21, p.24, with Lemmas 22 and 23.

assertions.value: The authors state quantum algorithms with time complexity O(poly log d) for solving the algebraic matrix Riccati equation for well-conditioned matrices, where a matrix A is well-conditioned if A ≥ I/(poly log d).
assertions.anchor: Section I A Summary of our results, p.6
quotes: We delineate quantum algorithms with time complexity O(poly log d) for solving Eq.
Here, we say a matrix A is well-conditioned if A ≥ I/(poly log d).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in Section I A and developed in Sections III B and III C; the proofs were not checked by the reader.
assertions.reader_inference: The O(poly log d) cost is for block-encoded outputs, not for reading out the solution.

assertions.value: The authors state that the assumptions under which a block-encoding of the Riccati solution can be constructed are not generally satisfied.
quotes: Although these assumptions are not generally satisfied, this still gives an idea of the extent and reach of the matrix geometric mean.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit on its own construction in Section VI.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike the output of most quantum algorithms for linear systems of equations, the solutions of the nonlinear matrix equations are not embedded in pure quantum states, but in terms of observables from which expectation values can be extracted.
quotes: Unlike the output of most quantum algorithms for linear systems of equations, these solutions of the nonlinear matrix equations are not embedded in pure quantum states, but rather in terms of observables from which we can extract expectation values.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the form of its own output in Section VI.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum learning advantage on a scalable photonic platform
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results text on Fig. 2 and Fig. 3, Outlook; supplementary material not in the file.
papers.what_it_is: An experiment on a continuous-variable photonic platform that uses entangled probe light to learn a multimode displacement process with fewer samples.

assertions.value: The authors report that with approximately 5 dB of two-mode squeezing they learn a 100-mode bosonic displacement process using 11.8 orders of magnitude fewer samples than a conventional scheme.
quotes: With approximately 5 dB of two-mode squeezing
we learn a 100-mode bosonic displacement process using 11.8 orders of magnitude fewer samples than a conventional scheme.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the entanglement-free sample complexity was estimated from an exponential fit of low mode number data as high as 7.3 × 1018 for the same task, and that the experiment does not demonstrate a provable quantum advantage for process reconstruction.
quotes: from an exponential fit of low mode number data, we estimate that the entanglement-free scheme using vacuum states and heterodyne measurements would require a sample complexity as high as 7.3 × 1018 for the same task
Therefore, the improved process reconstruction we achieved using entanglement does not demonstrate a provable quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its baseline is obtained and the limit of the reconstruction claim, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors report, for the largest 120-mode experiment, a hypothesis testing success probability of 0.563 ± 0.025, exceeding the bound for a conventional strategy (0.5 + 3.8 × 10−11) with a confidence level of 99.3%, and state that this indicates a provable quantum advantage of 9.2 orders of magnitude.
assertions.anchor: Section on hypothesis testing, Fig. 3(d), p.5
quotes: For the largest scale (120-mode) experiment, we measured a hypothesis testing success probability of 0.563 ± 0.025, exceeding the bound for conventional strategy (0.5 + 3.8 × 10−11) with a confidence level of 99.3%.
Our result thus indicates a provable quantum advantage of 9.2 orders of magnitude.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experiment; the classical bound is theoretical, the measurement is empirical.

assertions.value: The authors state that the platform is scalable, albeit noisy and lossy, with system losses of approximately 20%.
quotes: we have demonstrated a substantial quantum advantage in learning using a scalable, albeit noisy and lossy, photonic platform
Despite system losses of approximately 20%
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the condition of its own platform in the Outlook.
